extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and inventors studying patentability principles
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the legal qualities of invention for patentability: how novelty, application, claims, materials, and prior art determine whether an improvement or use is patentable. Draws on case law illustrations and claim-construction rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty — new, useful, and different in substance
rubrics_metrics.description: “The question is not whether the invention is better or worse than its predecessors, but whether it is new, useful, and different from any thing before used or known.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test novelty by asking whether the claimed invention is materially different in substance (not merely in form) from prior art. (Illustrated by bed-plate/engine case where differences were 'radical in their character' and sustained validity.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation / prior use defeats patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior device or combination substantially anticipates the claimed construction or arrangement, the patent is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Stimpson v. Woodman — the claimed machine was anticipated except for figures on a roller; the substitution or engraving did not create patentable novelty. If every essential part was found in earlier devices, claim fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere mechanical skill or substitution is not invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes that 'involved simply mechanical skill' (e.g., stamping a figure on a roller or substituting an old figured roller) are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the only difference from prior art is a routine mechanical change or simple substitution of an old element, courts treat it as non-inventive and deny protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of invention and specification limits (claims limited by description)
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement is to be confined by the specification and description; claims are interpreted in view of what the specification states (e.g., limited to cast-iron guns because the specification mentioned cast iron).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treadwell v. Parrott: claim confined to cast-iron guns because the specification limited the invention to that material; thus claims must be read in light of the specification's expressed scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of an old contrivance to a new use (double use) is generally not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a well-known mode of manufacture or contrivance to a new occasion or use (a 'double use') does not ordinarily constitute patentable invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: anchors made by an old manufacturing principle applied to ship's anchors; rocking-chair example; medicines applied to new disease. If the new use is merely analogous to prior uses, courts treat it as non-inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of material alone is not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply substituting one material for another (e.g., making door-knobs of porcelain instead of wood or iron) is not an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the sole change is material substitution without new method, combination, or effect, courts have held the subject not patentable (Hotchkiss v. Greenwood style reasoning).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect-versus-occasion test — the effect must be new, not only the occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the use produces an effect 'of itself entirely new' or whether only the occasion/purpose is new; if only the occasion is new and effect is analogous, no invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: use of gas to singe lace produced a non-analogous, new effect and was patentable; using known scissors on a different but analogous material would not be patentable. Great discrimination required in assessing analogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: New combinations, contrivances, or arrangements of known agents can be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when principal agents are known, if new contrivances, combinations, or arrangements are employed they may constitute a new principle and be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include different combinations in manufacturing (e.g., anthracite with hot-air blast in iron manufacture). Courts will protect new organizational or structural changes that produce new results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper claim drafting: overly broad or imprecise claims can forfeit patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that improperly describe the invention or hazard the patentable quality (e.g., claiming the mode of using a caisson rather than the specific machine) can render an otherwise new invention unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caisson example: the patentee's broad claim to the mode of construction risked the patent because the apparatus and parts of the claimed method were already known; claims should accurately and narrowly describe the inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty is contextual to the history of the art (inventor’s relation to prior knowledge matters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether something is patentable depends in part on the inventor's position relative to prior art — a new application may be only a double use if the method/principle was known elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a method/principle has been discovered/applied before (even in different materials or contexts), later application may not be patentable unless it produces a new effect or employs new means.

rubrics_metrics.name: New manufacture by old process or old manufacture by new means — assess newness of result or means
rubrics_metrics.description: If a new manufacture is produced by an old process, or an old manufacture is produced by new means, the case may be patentable — the decisive question is whether the result or means is new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the result/effect is genuinely new (even if some parts are old), patent may be proper; conversely, producing an old result by means analogous to prior art will not suffice. (See discussions of when maceration + spinning produced a new manufacture.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovering a previously unknown capacity or mode of using an existing machine may be patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: If one discovers a new way of using a machine that the world had not known before (e.g., adjusting rollers to an unexpected ratch yielding a new manufacture), that discovery may be patentable even without new parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kay v. Marshall nuance: if the capacity of the existing spinning-machine to be used at a certain ratch was previously unknown and the inventor discovered it, that new use (if genuinely novel) could justify a patent for the new application or for an improved machine as to its functional relations.
